18 1 2221 -1962 

Indian Standard 

METHODS OF TEST FOR 
AMINOPLASTIC MOULDING MATERIALS 

0. FOREWORD 

0*1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution 
on 8 August 1962, after the draft finalized by the Plastics Sectional 
Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 

0.2 The commercially important aminoplastics are the urea-formaldehyde 
and melamine formaldehyde condensates. The applications of aminoplastic 
resins in paper manufacture, textiles, adhesives, enamels and lacquers and 
in moulding has increased greatly in recent years. 

0*3 In the preparation of this standard, assistance has been derived from 
B.S. 1322 : 1956 Aminoplastics Moulding Materials, issued by the British 
Standards Institution. 

0.4 The International Organization for Standardization ( ISO ) has 
published the following ISO Recommendations in the field of testing of 
aminoplastic moulding materials: 

ISO/R 60 Plastics. Determination or Apparent Density of 
Moulding Material that can be Poured from a Speci- 
fied Funnel. 

ISO/R 62 Plastics. Determination of Water Absorption. 

ISO/R 117 Plastics. Determination of Boiling Water Absorp- 
tion of Plastics. 

ISO/R 171 Plastics. Determination of Bulk Factor of Mould- 
ing Materials. 

ISO/R 180 Plastics. Determination of the Izod Impact Resis- 
tance of Rigid Plastics. 

The corresponding methods of test given in this standard agree with these 
ISO Recommendations. 

0.5 Wherever a reference to any Indian Standard appears in this standard, 
it shall be taken as a reference to the latest version of the standard. 

0.6 Metric system has been adopted in India and all quantities and 
dimensions in this standard have been given in this system. Non-metric 
values to which the industry has been accustomed are also given in 



IS: 2221- 1962 

brackets, wherever necessary, for the sake of smooth changeover by 
December 1966. 

0.7 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this 
standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated* express- 
ing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with 
IS: 2-1960 Rules for Rounding Off Numerical Values (Revised). The 
number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the 
same as that of the specified value in this standard. 

0.8 This standard is intended chiefly to cover the technical provisions 
relating to the methods of test for aminoplastic moulding materials, and it 
does not include all the necessary provisions of a contract. 



1. SCOPE 

1.1 This standard prescribes the methods of test for aminoplastic moulding 
materials. It prescribes the methods for determining apparent powder 
density, density of moulding and bulk factor, mould shrinkage, water 
absorption, boiling water absorption, degree of cure, tensile strength, 
impact strength, plastic yield, cross-breaking strength, electric strength at 
90 C, surface resistivity, volume resistivity, and resistance to tracking. 

1.2 Should any inconsistency be found to exist between the methods 
prescribed in this standard and those in the standard for individual 
materials, the latter shall prevail. 

2. TERMINOLOGY 

2.0 For the purpose of tnis standard, the following definitions shall apply. 

2.1 Aminoplastic — Plastics based on resins made by the condensation of 
amines, such as urea, thiourea, melamine or allied compounds ( such as 
cyanamide polymers and diaminotriazines ) with aldehydes, particularly 
formaldehyde. 

2.2 Apparent Powder Density — The weight of a unit volume of the 
loose material under prescribed conditions. 

2.3 Breathing ( or Gassing ) — The operation of opening a mould for a 
very short period of time at an early stage in the process of cure. 
Breathing allows the escape of gas and vapour from the moulding material 
and reduces the tendency of thick mouldings to blister. 



IS: 2221. 1962 

2.4 Bulk Factor — The ratio of the density of a moulding to the apparent 
powder density of the moulding material from which it was made. This 
ratio is numerically equal to the ratio of the volumes of equal weights of the 
material in unmoulded and moulded form* 

2.5 Cross-Breaking Strength — The empirical maximum stress in a 
beam at failure in bend. It is numerically equal to maximum bending 
moment at failure divided by modulus of section, but the calculated value 
does not represent the true maximum surface stress because the method of 
calculation holds good only for an ideal elastic solid. 

2.6 Coring Time ( or Cure Time ) — In the process of moulding, it is 
the interval of time between the instant of final cessation of relative move- 
ment between the moving parts of the mould and the instant the pressure 
is released. 

2.7 Density of Moulding — The weight of a unit volume of the moulded 
material without inserts. 

2.8 Dwelling—- A pause in the application of pressure to a mould, made 
just before the mould is completely closed, to allow the escape of gas from 
the moulding material. 

2 3 Electric Strength at 90°C — The maximum voltage which the test 
specimen can withstand for a specified period of time without breakdown 
divided by the thickness of the specimen in millimetres. 

2.10 Flash Mould — A mould so designed that when charged with an 
excess moulding material, the excess escapes at the space in between the 
relatively moving parts of the mould. This excess or ' flash ' sustains part 
of the total applied pressure. 

2.11 Impact Strength — The energy required to fracture the test speci- 
men under prescribed conditions. 

2*12 Melamine Formaldehyde Resin — A synthetic resin derived from 
the reaction of melamine ( 2,4,6-triamino-l,3,5-triazine ) with formaldehyde 
or its polymers. 

2.13 Moulding «*- The shaped article manufactured from a moulding 
material which has been cured by heat and pressure in a mould. It 
includes any metal or other accessories inserted during the process of 
moulding. The moulding may be in the condition in which it was taken 
from the mould or may have been trimmed, machined or polished 
subsequently. 

244 Moulding Material* Urea — The uncured composition containing 
urea synthetic resins, various fillers and other ingredients, which becomes 
hard, infusible and insoluble ( that if, cured) by the application of heat 



18 1 2221- 1962 

fend pressure. The material may be in powder, flake or granular form 
or these forms compressed to pellets, tablets or preforms* 

2.15 Mould Shrinkage — The difference in dimensions, expressed in 
thousandths of millimetre per millimetre ( or in mils per inch ) between a 
moulding and the mould cavity in which it was moulded, both the mould 
and moulding being at normal room temperature when measured. 

2*16 Plastic Yield — Non- elastic deformation of a sample beam at a given 
temperature under given load. 

2.17 Positive Mould — A mould in which the total applied pressure rests 
only and continuously on the moulding and from which no excess mould* 
ing material or flash can escape during the moulding process. 

2*18 Semt*positive Mould — A mould which is built on positive lines but 
which allows a limited amount of escape of the flash as the mould is 
closed. 

2.19 Surface Resistivity — The electrical resistance on the surface of 
the material between the opposite sides of one centimetre square of the 
test specimen. 

2.20 Synthetic Resin Urea — A resin produced by the condensation of 
urea with aldehydes. 

2.21 Tensile Strength — The maximum tensile load sustained by the test 
specimen under prescribed conditions divided by the original cross* 
sectional area of the specimen. 

2*22 Thieurea-Formaldehyde Resin— -A synthetic resin derived from 
the reaction of thiourea ( thiocarbamide ) with formaldehyde. 

2*23 Ure*-Formaldehyde Resin — A synthetic resin derived from the 
reaction of urea ( carbamide ) with formaldehyde or its polymers. 

2.24 Volume Resistivity — The electrical resistance of a unit volume of 
one centimetre cube measured between the opposite faces. 

3. SAMPLING 

3.1 Sampling shall be carried out as prescribed in IS : 2213-1962 Methods 
of Sampling of Thermosetting Moulding Materials. 

4. DETERMINATION OP APPARENT POWDER DENSITY 

4.1 Carry out the determination in duplicate. 
4*2 Apparatus 
4*2.1 Funml — of the shape and dimensions shown in Fig* 1 » 

7 



13 1 2221- 1962 

4.2.2 Cylindrical Measure — may be constructed of metal and having 
internal diameter 40 mi&, height 80 mm and capacity 100*0 ± 0*5 ml. 



H 56 




U-33 -J 
All dimensions in millimetre!. 
Fio. 1 Funnel for Determining Apparent Powder Density 



4*3 Procedure — Mix well the sample of the material before test. 
Support the funnel vertically with its lower orifice 20 to 30 mm above and 
coaxial with the cylindrical measure. With the lower orifice of the funnel 
closed by any convenient means, place a quantity of the material exceeding 
100 ml in it. Allow the material to flow into the cylinder. If necessary, 
assist the flow of the material by loosening it with a rod. When the 
cylinder is full, draw a blade with a straight edge across its top to remove 
excess material. Weigh the contents of the cylindrical measure to the 
nearest 0*1 g. 

4.4 Calculation and Report — Calculate to two places of decimal the 
apparent powder density, that is, the weight in grams of 1 ml of the 
material. The mean of the duplicate determination shall be taken as the 
representative value of apparent powder density of the test sample. 

5. DETERMINATION OF DENSITY OF MOULDING AND BULK 
FACTOR 

5.1 Carry out the determination on two test specimens prepared from the 
same test sample material. 

8 



IS j 2221- 1962 

5.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The test specimens shall be in 
the form of moulded discs 50*0 db 1-0 mm ( or 2'00 ± 0-04 in ) in diameter 
and 30 ± 0*2 mm ( or (H25 =fc 0*010 in ) thick. 

5.2.1 Mould the discs in a positive or a semi-positive mould, with a 
moulding pressure 315 to 472 kg/cm 1 (or 2 to 3 ton/in 8 ) and mould 
temperature 135° to 150°C. If desired, pre-heat the moulding material 
before loading into the mould. The period of time elapsing between 
the filling of the mould and commencement of the pressure increase shall 
be 15 db 2 seconds. Do not allow the moulding time to exceed 10 minutes; 
but less time may be used provided the specimen is properly cured. If 
found necessary, chill the mould before ejection of the moulding. Cool 
the specimen to room temperature. Test it within 24 hours to moulding. 

5.3 Procedure — Weigh a piece of wire of sufficient length to reach from 
the hook of the pan supports to the beaker support. Attach the test 
specimen to the wire so as to suspend about 25 mm above the beaker 
support and weigh it. Weigh the specimen again while immersed with the 
wire in distilled water at 27 A 2°C. Make sure that there are no air 
bubbles on the surface of the specimen and the wire while immersed in 
water* 

5*4 Calculation sad Report 

5.4.1 Density of Moulding —For the degree of accuracy required, the 
density of water at 27*C may be taken as 1*0 g/ml. Buoyancy corrections 
may be neglected. 



W 
Density of moulding ( g/ml ) at 27°C ^-fir^ — 



where 

W «■ weight in g of specimen in air, and 
w «* weight in g of specimen in water. 

Round off the calculated value of density of moulding to two places of 
decimal. The mean of the two determinations shall be taken as the 
representative value of density of moulding for the test sample. 

5*4.2 Bulk Factor — Calculate the bulk factor by dividing the repre- 
sentative value of the density of moulding by the representative value 
of apparent powder density, the result being rounded off to the second 
place of decimal, 

6. DETERMINATION OF MOULD SHRINKAGE 

6.1 Carry out the determination on two test specimens prepared from 
the same test sample material. 



IS 1 2221-1962 

6.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The test specimens shall be in the 
form of moulded discs 1000 db 1*0 mm ( or 4*00 dk 0*04 in ) in diameter 
and 3*0 & 0*2 mm ( or 0*125 db 0*010 in ) thick, and shall be Hat. 

6.2*1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould with 
a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm 2 ( or 2 to 3 ton/in 1 ) and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150°C. Do not pre-hcat the moulding material 
before loading into the mould and allow the mould to breathe. The 
period of time elapsing between the filling of the mould and the com- 
mencement of the pressure increase shall be 15 ± 2 seconds. Mould the 
specimen for 4*00 db 0*25 minutes, eject the moulding hot and allow to 
cool to 27 ± 2°C and measure the dimensions. 

6.3 Calculation — Calculate the mould shrinkage by substracting the 
diameter of the cold moulding from that of the cold mould and divide 
by the diameter of the cold mould, the measurements being made on a 
marked diameter to avoid possible inaccuracy due to the specimen not 
being perfectly circular. Express the mould shrinkage in thousandths of 
millimetre per millimetre ( or mils per inch ). 

6.4 Report — The mean of the two determinations shall be taken as the 
representative value of mould shrinkage for the test sample. 

7. DETERMINATION OF WATER ABSORPTION 

7.1 Carry out the determination on three test specimens prepared from the 
same test sample material. 

7.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The specimens shall be in the 
form of moulded discs 50*0 J- 1*0 mm ( or 2*00 =b 0*04 in ) in diameter and 
>0 ± 0*2 mm ( or 0-125 ± 0*010 in ) thick. 

Note — Comparison of water absorption values k possible only when specimens of 
identical dimensions are used. 

7.2.1 Mould the discs in a positive or semi-positive mould, with a 
moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* (or 2 to 3 ton/in 2 ) and mould 
temperature to 135 to 150°C. If desired, prc-heat the moulding powder 
before loading into the mould. The period of time elapsing between the 
filling of the mould and the commencement of the pressure increase shall 
be 15 ± 2 seconds. The moulding conditions shall be such as to give 
moulding free from porosity. They shall be cured for the minimum time 
required to be properly cured when tested by the method prescribed in 9. 

Note — With increasing curing time, the cold water absorption of urea mouldings 
normally increases and the boiling water absorption decreases. 

7.5 Procedure — Dry the specimens in an oven for 24 ± 1 hours 
at 50 ± 3°C, cool in a desiccator and weigh to the nearest milligram 

10 



IS:2221-1962 

(W'i). Immediately, place them in a container of distilled water 
maintained at 27*0 ± 0*5°C. Take precautions to prevent specimens from 
making contact over any substantial area with one another or with the 
container. Take the specimens away from water one by one after 
24 ± 1 hours and remove all surface water with a clean dry cloth or with 
filter paper. Re-weigh the specimens within one minute of taking them 
out from water ( W % ). 

7.3.1 When it is desired to allow for the presence of water-soluble 
matter* re-dry the specimens in an oven for 24 ± 1 hours at 50 ± 3°C 
after completing the procedure prescribed under 7*3, cool in a desiccator 
and re- weigh ( W z ). 

7.4 Calculation and Report — The water absorption of a test specimen 
is the difference in milligrams between the weight after immersion and the 
weight before immersion, that is, ( W t — W x ). The mean of the three 
determinations shall be taken as the representative value of water absorp- 
tion for the test sample. 

7.4.1 When allowing for the presence of water-soluble matter, the water 
absorption of a test specimen is the difference in milligrams between the 
weight after immersion and the weight after re-drying, that is, ( W % — W\ }. 
The mean of the three determinations shall be taken as the representative 
value of water absorption for the test sample. 

8. DETERMINATION OF BOILING WATER ABSORPTION 

8.1 Carry out the test on at least two test specimens prepared from the 
same test sample material. 

8.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The test specimens shall be 
moulded discs 50'0± 1-0 mm (or 2 % 00 ± 0*04 in) in diameter and 
30 ± 0-2 mm ( or 0-125 ± 0*010 in ) thick. 

8.2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or semi-positive mould with a 
moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm 2 ( or 2 to 3 ton/in 8 ) of such lower 
pressure as can be shown to give results of the same order, and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150*0. It is permissible to pre-heat the material 
before loading into the mould. Breathing or dwelling when necessary 
arc permitted. The period of time elapsing between the filling of the 
mould and the commencement of the pressure increase shall be 15 ± 2 
seconds. The moulding conditions shall be such as to give mouldings 
free from porosity. The mouldings shall be cured for the minimum time 
required to be properly cured when tested by the method prescribed in 9. 
The conditions used for moulding the test specimens for the test for boiling 
water absorption and for cold water absorption {see 7) shall be the same. 

il 



IS t2221-1962 

8.3 Procedure 

8.3.1 Place the specimen in an oven at 50 ± 3°C for 24 ± 1 hours, 
cool in a desiccator and weigh immediately ( W x ). Then totally immerse 
the specimen in boiling distilled water for 30 ± 1 minutes, supporting in 
such a way that the water has free aceess to both faces. Plunge the 
specimen into water at 27 ± 2°C for 15 ± 1 minutes. Re* weigh the 
specimen within one minute after removal of surplus water with a filter or 
blotting paper ( W % ). 

8.3.2 Keep the specimen again for 24 hours at 50 ± 3°C, cool in a 
desiccator and re- weigh immediately ( W % }. 

8.4 Calculation — If W % is less than W x ( indicating the presence of 
water-soluble or volatile matter), the boiling water absorption of the 
specimen is W t — W r If W* is greater than W %% the boiling water 
absorption of the specimen is W t — W v 

8.5 Report — The mean of the two determinations, expressed in milli- 
grams, shall be taken as the representative value of boiling water absorp- 
tion for the test sample. 

9. TEST FOR DEGREE OF CURE 

9.0 The method described in 9.1 is applicable to all types of amino- 
plasties, while the methods described in 9.2 provide a test for degree of 
cure for only mdamine-formaldehyde plastics and enable results to be 
interpreted easily. 

9.1 For All Types of Aminoplaatlc Mouldings 

9.1.1 Pw*di*r#~Saw the moulding to be tested through its thickest 
section and then immerse in boiling water for 10 minutes. Care shall be 
taken to see that the mouldings do not rest or lie with flat faces together 
during immersion; the whole surface of each moulding shall be freely 
exposed to the test water during the whole period of the test. 

9.1.1.1 The moulding shall be deemed to be properly cured if the 
surface is not adversely affected in appearance and cannot be scratched 
anywhere with a finger nail immediately after the immersion. 

9.2 For Melamine Formaldehyde Mouldings Only 
9 .2.1 Sulphuric AM Test 

9.2.1.1 Reagent 

a) Sulphuric acid— one percent ( wjv ). 

9.2.1.2 Procedure — Boil the moulding to be tested in sulphuric acid 
for 10 minutes. A cured moulding will not be affected by this treatment, 
whereas an uncured moulding will show localized patches of chalkiness. 

12 



IS: 2221 -1962 

9*2.2 Dye Test 

9.2.2.1 Reagent 

a) Rhodamine-B solution — - 0*01 percent, freshly prepared. 

9.2 .2.2 Procedure — Immerse the moulding to be tested for 10 minutes 
in boiling rhodamine-B solution. An improperly cured moulding will 
show intense staining by the dyestuff by this treatment, while a properly 
cured moulding will remain unchanged in colour except at the flash lines. 

10. DETERMINATION OF TENSILE STRENGTH 

10*1 Garry out the determination on three test specimens prepared from 
the same test sample material. 

10.2 Preparation of Teat Specimens — The test specimens shall conform 
to dimensions shown in Fig. 2.

Fio. 2 Specimen foe Tensile Test 



10*2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould, 
with a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm 2 ( or 2 to 3 ton/in 1 ) and 
mould temperature of 135 to 150°C, the direction of moulding pressure 
being as shown in Fig. 2. If desired, pre-heat the powder before loading 
into the mould. The period of time elapsing between the filling of the 
mould and the commencement erf* the pressure increase shall be

15 i 2 seconds. Do not allow the curing time to exceed 15 minutes; but

specimen to room temperature. Note that all surfaces of the specimen are 
free from visible flaws, scratches or imperfections. Test the specimen within 
24 hours of moulding. 

10J Conditioning — Keep the test specimens in a desiccator over 
anhydrous calcium chloride for at least 16 hours before testing. 

10*3*1 Special conditioning procedure may be adopted if so agreed to 
between the purchaser and the supplier. 

10.4 Procedure — Allow a definite time interval, not exceeding 
60 minutes, to elapse between removal of the sample from the desiccator 
and application of load. Measure the width and the thickness of the 
specimen at several places near the centre of the specimen* Use any 
standard tensile testing machine provided the load at fracture can be 
measured to within one percent. Hold the specimen even and firmly in 
grips as shown in Fig. 3 f Increase the load evenly so that the specimen 
breaks within 0*5 to 1*5 minutes from the start of the loading. Record 
the maximum load sustained by the specimen during the test.

11. DETERMINATION OF IMPACT STRENGTH 

11.1 Garry out the determination on at least five test specimens prepared 
from the same test sample material. 

11.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The moulded ( or moulded and 
then machined ) specimens shall conform to dimensions shown in Fig. 4, 
except that the notched face and the face opposite to it shall be moulded 
surfaces. 

11.2*1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould, 
with a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* (or 2 to 3 ton/in 2 ) and 
mould temperature of 135 to 150°C, the direction of moulding pressure 
being as shown in Fig. 4. If desired, pre-heat the powder before loading 
into the mould. Dwelling and breathing are permitted. The period of 
time elapsing between the filling of the mould and the commencement of 
the pressure increase shall be 15 ±2 seconds. The moulding conditions 
shall be such as to give mouldings properly cured and free from porosity. 
Cool the specimens to room temperature. Test it within 24 hours of 
moulding.

11,3.1 Special conditioning procedure may be adopted if so agreed

11.4 Procedure 

11.4.1 Accurately mount the specimen in the vice of a pendulum ( Tzod ) 
type impact testing machine as shown in Fig. 5, with the notch facing

the striker and the root of the notch level with .the horizontal face of the 
vice. Strike the specimen at a distance of 22*0 ± 0*5 mm ( or 0*866 ± 
0*020 in ) from the face of the vice, the velocity of the striking edge at the 
moment of impact being 2 440 ± 30 mm ( or 8*0 ± 0*1 ft ) per second. 

11.4.2 The gripping edge of the vice shall have a radius of approxi- 
mately 0*4 mm (or 1/64 in). The pendulum shall be so constructed 
that the centre of percussion coincides with the centre of the striking 
edge. This edge shall have a radius of 3*2 mm (or 1/8 in) and shall 
strike squarely across the full width of the specimen. The machine 
shall be solidly constructed and the striking energy shall be 0*14 kg.m 
(or lft lb).

12. DETERMINATION OF PLASTIC YIELD 

12.1 Carry out the determination on two test specimens prepared from 
the same test sample material. 

12.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The test specimens shall 
conform to dimensions shown in Fig. 6.

OIRECTIOM OF 

MOULDING PRESSURE

P-ts-0!3 



All dimensions in millimetres. 
Fxo. 6 Specimen for Plastic Yield Test 

12.2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould, with 
a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* ( or 2 to 3 ton/in* ) and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150 P C, the direction of moulding pressure being as 
shown in Fig. 6. If desired, pre-heat the powder before loading into the 
mould. The period of time elapsing between the filling of the mould and 
the commencement of the pressure increase shall be 15 ± 2 seconds. Do 
not allow the curing time to exceed 15 minutes; but less time may be used 
provided the specimen is properly cured. If found necessary, chill the 
mould before ejection of the moulding. Cool the specimen to room 
temperature. Test the specimen within 24 hours of moulding. 

12.3 Procedure 

12.3.1 Carry out the test in an oven maintained within ± 2°C of the 
temperature specified in the individual standard for moulding powder. 
Fix the specimen in a rigid manner in the oven by means of a clamp as 
shown in Fig. 7, and suspend a suitable stirrup with a rigid knife-edge, 
carrying an attachment for supporting the weight from the notch in the 
unsupported end of the specimen. Do not allow the weight of the stirrup 
and attachment to exceed 20 g.

7 Arrangement of Specimen for Plastic Yield Test 



12.3.2 Fifteen minutes after placing the specimen in the oven, measure 
the height of the unsupported end of the specimen with reference to a 
suitable datum point in millimetres to an accuracy of 0*1 mm in such a 
manner that the temperature of the oven does not (all below the specified 
limit while the measurement is being taken. Then attach a weight to the 
stirrup so that the total load, including the stirrup, applied to the speci- 
men is 450 ± 1 g. Maintain the specimen in the oven under these condi- 
tions for 6 hours ±10 minutes. At the end of this period, again 
measure the height of the unsupported end of the specimen with reference 
to the datum point, while the specimen is under the test conditions of load 
and temperature. 

12.4 Calculation mud Report — Record the difference between the 
initial and final measurements expressed in millimetres. The mean of the 
two determinations shall be taken as the representative value of plastic 
yield for the test-material. 

13. DETERMINATION OF CROSS-BREAKING STRENGTH 

13.1 Carry out the determination on three test specimens prepared from 
the same test sample material. 

13.2 Preparation of Teat Specimens — The specimens shall consist of 
moulded rectangular bars of length 114 mm ( or 4*5 in ) minimum, width 
12-7 ± 0-2 mm ( or 0*500 ± 0010 in ) and thickness 9*5 ± 0*2 mm ( or 
0-375 ±0-010 in), 

13.2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould, with 
a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* ( or 2 to 3 ton/in* ) and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150°C- Apply the moulding pressure in a direction 
perpendicular to the largest face of the specimen. If desired, pre-heat the 



18 



IS 1 2221 -1962 

powder before loading into the mould. The period of time elapsing 
between the filling of the mould and the commencement of the pressure 
increase shall be 15 ± 2 seconds. Do not allow the curing time to exceed 
8 minutes; but less time may be used provided the specimen is properly 
cured. If found necessary, chill the mould before ejection of the moulding. 
Cool the specimen to room temperature and test it within 24 hours of 
moulding. 

13.3 Procedure — Determine the mean breadth and the mean thickness 
of the specimen. Place the specimen symmetrically across parallel 
V-shaped supports, the distance between the supporting edges being 
101-6 ± 0-2 mm (or 4*000 ± 0*010 in). Apply a load squarely across 
the breadth of the specimen by means of a third V-shaped block parallel 
to and midway between the supporting blocks. The contact edges of the 
supporting blocks and the block applying the load shall have a radius of 
approximately 1*6 mm ( or ^ in ). Increase the load steadily so that the 
specimen fractures in 15 to 45 seconds. Note the load in kilograms at 
failure.

D ■* mean thickness in cm of specimen. 

13.5 Report — The mean of the three determinations shall be taken as 
the representative value of cross-breaking strength for the test sample. 

14. DETERMINATION OF ELECTRIC STRENGTH AT 90°C 

14*1 Carry out the determination on at least four test specimens prepared 
from the same test sample material. One of these specimens shall be used 
merely to provide a preliminary estimate of the probable value of the 
voltage at which other specimens are likely to fail. 

14.2 Preparation of Test Specimen* — The specimens shall be mould- 
ed discs 1000 ± l'O mm ( or 4*00 ± 0*04 in ) in diameter and 3'0 ± 0*2 mm 
( or 0*125 ± 0*010 in ) thick. The specimens shall be flat. 

14.2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or semi-positive mould with a 
moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* (or 2 to 3 ton/in 1 ) and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150°C. If desired, pre-heat the powder before 
loading into the mould. The period of time elapsing between the filling 

19 



IS s 2221- 1962 

of the mould and the commencement of the pressure increase shall be 
15 ± 2 seconds. Do not allow the curing time to exceed 6 minutes; but 
less time may be used provided the specimen is properly cured. If found 
necessary, chill the mould before ejection of the moulding. Cool the 
specimen to room temperature and test it within 24 hours of moulding. 

14.3 Conditioning — Keep the specimens for at least 5 hours in a 
desiccator over anhydrous calcium chloride at room temperature prior 
to testing. 

14.4 Apparatus 

14.4.1 Electrodes — The bottom electrode shall consist of a solid cylinder 
of brass 80 mm ( or 3 in ) in diameter and 25 mm ( or 1 in ) in thickness. 
The upper electrode shall consist of a solid cylinder of brass 40 mm 
(or 1*5 in ) in diameter and 40 mm ( or 1 # 5 in ) in thickness. The sharp 
edges of the electrodes shall be rounded to a radius not exceeding 0*8 mm 
(or 0*031 in). The test faces shall be kept smooth and polished and 
free from pitting. The electrodes shall be held truly coaxial while 
testing. 

14.4.2 Testing Transformer — Alternating voltage, approximately of the 
sine-wave form and of 50 c/s frequency shall be used. The wave-form of 
the test voltage shall not vary by more than ±5 percent from a pure sine- 
wave (that is, the crest factor shall be within 1*343 to 1*484). The rms 
value of the applied voltage shall be determined from the readings of a 
peak voltmeter suitably connected to the output side of the transformer. 
For this purpose, the wave-form shall be deemed to the sinusoidal; ( The 
rms value may also be determined by an electrostatic voltmeter connected 
to the output side or even by an ordinary ac voltmeter connected to the 
input side or to a tertiary coil, provided that this voltmeter has been 
properly calibrated against a sphere gap connected to the output side. ) 
The capacity of the transformer shall be sufficient to maintain the full test 
voltage on the specimen for the maximum time required for the test. A 
rating of 2 to 5 kVA depending upon the output voltage shall normally be 
considered sufficient. The transformer circuit should be protected from 
excessive current by a circuit-beaker on breakdown of the test specimen. 

14.4.3 Voltage Control — Control of voltage may be secured by using one 
of the following devices: 

a) Variable ratio auto-transformer, 

b) Induction regulator, 

c) Generator field regulator ( for separate alternator ), and 

d) Resistance potential divider. 

20 



18:2221-1962 

14.5 Procedure 

14*5.1 Immerse at least four specimens and the electrodes for 15 to 
25 minutes in a bath of insulating oil [ conforming to *IS : 335-1953 Speci- 
fication for Insulating Oil for Transformers and Switchgear ( Low Viscosity 
Type ) ] maintained at 90 ± 2°C. At the end of this time, apply a voltage 
to one specimen mounted symmetrically between the electrodes as shown in 
Fig. 8 and increase it uniformly at about 30 W per minute until break- 
down occurs. Treat this as a preliminary estimate of the probable value 
of the voltage at which other specimens are likely to fafl. Mount the 
remaining three specimens in turn between the electrodes and apply a 
voltage equal approximately to half the breakdown voltage of the first 
specimen and maintain for 20 seconds. If the specimen withstands this 
voltage without failure, raise the test voltage in steps of 1 kV uo to 25 kV 
and thereafter in steps of 2 kV. H

14.5.2 Maintain each test voltage for 20 seconds unless failure occurs. 
If the second or any subsequent specimens fail in less than 20 seconds at 
the commencement of the testing, disregard the test and repeat it on a 
fresh specimen, the initially applied voltage stress being approximately one- 
fourth of the breakdown voltage of the first specimen in this case. 

14.6 Calculation — The electric strength of the specimen shall be the 
maximum voltage which the specimen withstands for 20 seconds with- 
out breakdown, divided by the thickness of the specimen in millimetres 
measured near the point of breakdown.

15. DETERMINATION OF SURFACE RESISTIVITY AFTER 
IMMERSION IN WATER 

15.1 Carry out the determination on at least two test specimens prepared 
from the same test sample material. 

15.2 Preparation of Test Specimens — The specimens shall be 
moulded discs 100*0 ± 1*0 mm (or 4*00 ± 0-04 in) in diameter and 
3-0 ± 0-2 mm ( or 0*125 ± 0*010 in ) thick. The specimens shall be flat. 

15.2.1 Mould the specimens in a positive or a semi-positive mould, with 
a moulding pressure of 315 to 472 kg/cm* ( or 2 to 3 ton/in* ) and mould 
temperature of 135 to 150*C. If desired, pre-heat the material before 
loading into the mould. The period of time elapsing between the filling 
of the mould and the commencement of the pressure increase shall be 
15 db 2 seconds. Do not allow the curing time to exceed 6 minutes; but 
less time may be used provided the specimen is properly cured. If found 
necessary, chill the mould before ejection of the moulding. Cool the 
specimen to room temperature and test it within 24 hours of moulding. 

15.3 Conditioning — Immerse the specimens for 24'0 =fc 0*5 hours in 
distilled water at a temperature of 27 db 2°C. Take out the specimens 
from water and remove all surface moisture by pressing with dry blotting 
or filter paper. 

J5.4 Apparatus — Electrodes as shown in Fig- 9 and the circuit as shown 
in Fig. 10 are suitable for measuring surface resistivity. 

15.5 Procedure — Measure the surface resistance of the specimen at 
27 ± 5°C in 10 to 15 minutes from the time of its removal from water. 
The relative humidity of the laboratory atmosphere at the time of test shall 
not exceed 75 percent. The surface resistance between the electrodes shall 
be measured one minute after the application of electrical pressure at 
500 ± 50 volts dc.

17. DETERMINATION OF RESISTANCE TO TRACKING 

17.1 Preparation of Test Specimen — Prepare a flat moulding contain- 
ing two metal inserts, a brass rod 5 mm ( or T 8 T in ) in diameter being 
suitable for the purpose. The metal inserts may be moulded in, or inserted 
afterwards into holes drilled or moulded for the purpose. They shall be 
32 mm ( or 1*25 in ) apart at the closest points. 

17.2 Procedure — Connect the metal electrodes to a 200 to 250 volts, 
50 cycles supply capable of giving at least 8 amperes, a 15- ampere fuse 
being included in the circuit. Pour on to the moulding a 10 percent 
solution of sodium chloride to flood the space between the electrodes. 
Switch on the current and maintain for 30 minutes, adding fresh salt solu- 
tion at 5 minute intervals. Examine the specimen for the formation of a 
conducting carbon track. After completion of 30 minute test, wash the 
specimen free from .salt by soaking in several changes of water, wipe off 
the surface moisture and measure insulation resistance between electrodes.
